Strong winds downed tree limbs that caused power outages in Naugatuck, Middlebury, and Woodbury.  About 6,700 customers in Naugatuck were without power.
Strong winds downed a tree onto a house and cars on Springside Avenue in New Haven.

Strong winds downed trees and tree limbs, that downed power lines in Danbury and Ridgefield.||Strong winds downed a tree, which knocked down wires onto and around a house at 88 Drum Hill Road in Wilton.
Strong winds downed tree limbs in Fairfield.||The ASOS at Sikorsky Airport in Bridgeport measured a peak gust to 46 mph at 1:39 pm EDT.
Strong winds downed a tree branch on a woman in the Bronx, who was taken to a hospital after receiving a minor injury to her head.

Strong winds downed trees and tree limbs in parts of the Williamsburg and Gravesend sections of Brooklyn.  In Bensonhurst, a tree fell on a house on 21st Avenue that caused structural damage.  Parts of Dyker Heights reported power failures.

Strong winds downed trees and tree branches which resulted in scattered power outages.  Most of LIPA's 20,000 power outages occurred in the town of North Hempstead, where more than 11,000 outages were reported.

Strong winds downed trees and tree limbs and caused scattered power outages.  Around 11 am EDT, police said that a tree fell on a moving car travelling west on Route 17A in Warwick.  A man and woman suffered minor injuries when their car overturned.  Orange and Rockland Utilities reported power outages in the town of Tuxedo.
Coastal flooding was reported at the intersection of Brookville Blvd and Rockaway Blvd, with one car stranded.
Route 7 in Kearney was reported closed due to coastal flooding.
Route 46 in Little Ferry was reported closed at the Hackensack River due to coastal flooding.
Route 7 in Kearney was closed from 8:30 pm (EDT) until 1000 pm (EDT) due to coastal flooding.

The Bayview section of Milford, and New Haven Avenue were flooded around the time of high tide.
Ram Island Drive on Shelter Island was closed due to coastal flooding. One vehicle had its engine stall while crossing the flooded roadway.
Dune Road was reported closed due to flooding.
A man surfing alone in the waters off Rockaway Beach drowned when his leg strap became tangled and rough surf pulled him underwater.

Severe beach erosion and cuts into the dunes occurred along the Atlantic Ocean facing beaches.||In the Town of Babylon...Ocean Parkway was left 150 ft. from tide line compared with 350 ft. previously.  Also an estimated 200,000 cubic yards of sand was lost along a 10,000 ft. stretch of beaches.  Damage estimates from locations in Southwest Suffolk County include $ 4 million at Gilgo Beach in Babylon and $ 4.2 million for Davis Park in Brookhaven.| |At Robert Moses Field 4, 15 ft. were cut into the dune line.  There was also erosion on the east side of Field 5.  Field 5 may have to be closed next summer due to the lack of beach.||At Davis Park on Fire Island, 70 percent of the sand added to the beach in a community funded project was swept away.

Severe beach erosion occurred along with cuts into the dunes across the Atlantic Ocean facing shoreline.||The surf carved into the dunes in front of the pavilion at Smith Point County Park.||In parts of East Hampton, Bridgehampton, and Quogue, as much as 50 ft. of dunes was eaten away by the high waves.||Damages include $ 5.5 million in Quogue and $ 3.9 million at Smith's Point.||In Wainscott, the pavement at the end of Beach Lane collapsed on November 14th.||In Bridgehampton, homes along Surfside Drive that once had wide dunes between them and the ocean now peek out onto the beach over narrow bands of dune grass.||In Quogue, the sand dunes were scoured out from beneath the municipal beach pavilion.
Route 7 was closed along the Hackensack River due to moderate tidal flooding.

A wind gust of 51 mph was measured by the Automated Surface Observing System at Meriden Markham Airport at 10:30 am.  A strong wind gust knocked a tree down onto a moving vehicle and injured a 44 year old woman on Saturday morning, November 28, 2009.  The vehicle was traveling along Kensington Avenue near the Westfield Meriden Mall.  The tree landed between the dash board and front seat.

A peak wind gust of 44 mph was measured by a mesonet station in Huntington Station.  Law enforcement reported downed tree limbs and trees in Fort Salonga and Stony Brook.  A tree fell on and damaged a pickup truck in Stony Brook.

Lightning struck a large tree in the back yard of 92 Grassy Hill Road around 4:30 am EST.  It traveled through the ground, blasted a hole through the basement wall, and displaced wooden panels in the interior portions of the house.  The sound was so loud that it damaged the hearing of a woman living in the house.

Heavy rain caused a vehicle to hydroplane on a road bank on Brushy Ridge in New Canaan, CT.  The vehicle over turned, and the driver was taken to Norwalk Hospital for treatment. ||A large tree fell down in Waveny Park in New Canaan due to a combination of heavy rain and gusty winds.
Heavy rain caused a vehicle to hydroplane on Piedmont Street, causing it to lose control and crash into two parked cars. The driver was taken to Saint Mary's Hospital to treat head injuries.
Strong winds combined with heavy rain downed numerous trees and power lines across Orange County causing around a thousand power outages.
Strong winds combined with heavy rain downed numerous trees and power lines across Rockland County causing around a thousand power outages.
The Saddle River at Lodi rose above its flood stage of 6.0 ft at 7:15am EST.  The river crested at 6.16 ft. at 9:15am, and returned within its banks at 10:30am.
Ten feet of dunes on the east side of Field 5 at Robert Moses State Park were carved away by high surf.

The ASOS at Bridgeport Connecticut reported a wind gust of 50 mph. Strong winds also resulted in widespread downed trees in Greenwich and Stamford, closing roads including Riversville, Glenville and Indian Head Roads. These high winds also downed a tree onto a Connecticut transit bus outside of Springdale School, closing Hope Street and injuring the driver.

The ASOS's at Meriden and New Haven airports measured wind gusts of 56 mph and 52 mph respectively. In Waterbury, there was a partial roof collapse of an apartment building at 121 Lounsbury Street due to the winds.

A 51 mph gust was reported at Groton/New London Airport. These strong winds also knocked a 75 foot tall Spruce tree onto a house at 147 Shore Road in Waterford which produced damage to the roof and front porch.

A gust to 61 mph was reported at Great Gull Island at 1053 am. These strong winds knocked down a tree in North Babylon. The tree took down a high tension wire which ignited a pickup truck. The truck fire occured on Wickfield Lane around 855 am.
A wind gust of 63 mph was measured in Bayville.
A large tree limb was reported down in Ridgewood.
A tree was reported down, blocking a driveway in Fairlawn.
Multiple trees were reported down on overhead wires in Goshen.
Golf ball size hail was reported in West Caldwell.
Penny size hail was reported in Woodcliff Lake.

Strong winds pushed over a tree in Paterson. The tree fell onto a car, a utility pole and a house on East 26th Street at 830 am. Extensive damage to a car occurred, and power was cut to the home. The home suffered minor damage.
A fatality occurred due to black ice. The fatal accident occurred at the intersection of Mastic Road and Herkimer Street in Mastic at 645 am on Monday December 7th.
Multiple car accidents eastbound near exit 63.
Forty three vehicle accidents town wide in Livingston from 11am to 12 am EST. I-280 closed both directions from Roseland to West Orange with 8 serious accidents in 15 minutes reported at 11 am EST.
Seventeen car accidents on Route 23 South in Wayne...with road closed in both directions repoted at 1040 AM EST. 11 accidents involving 50 cars in Totowa in a 27 minute span during this time as well.
Forty six people were injured in a 50 car pile up near the corner of route 110 and Indian Well Road around noon when freezing rain began. None of the injuries were life threatening.
Strong northwest winds behind deep low pressure over the western Atlantic Ocean ripped scores of bricks from a building on Pacific Steet in Brooklyn NY.  No one was injured.
Sidewalk bridging along Alcott Place collapsed, injuring one person.

Strong winds blew a piece of metal flashing the size of a car or about 5 feet by 20 feet off the steeple on St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church.  The church is located on Hillhouse Avenue and Temple Street, and the damage occurred around 7 pm.
Strong winds uprooted trees and knocked down electrical lines.  One tree fell down on to the roof of a house on Cambridge Drive in Smithtown.
Tree and power lines were downed onto a driveway.  A car was damaged.  The location was Greenwood Ave. in Waterbury CT.
Strong winds brought down scaffolding outside 433 Beach 40th Street around 12 noon in Rockaway Beach NY.
Strong winds knocked down numerous power lines and trees across the area.  In Griswold CT, many roads including Route 14 were closed because of fallen trees and power lines.

Strong winds knocked down numerous trees and power lines.  In Nyack, a tree knocked down a utility pole in the area of Flitt Street.  A tractor trailer was overturned on the Tappan Zee Bridge due to the high winds around noon.  Winds of 62 mph were reported at Westchester County Airport (KHPN) at 1:17 pm.
A 62 mph wind gust was reported at Westchester County Airport (KHPN) at 1:17 pm.  A six car Metro north train ran into a tree that had fallen on power lines near the Pleasantville station.

Numerous trees were downed in Paramus NJ.  Two houses in Paramus were damaged by large tree limbs.  Also in Paramus, the 34 year old mayor of Paramus, male, suffered minor injuries due to a live wire touching a metal fence. Another Tree limb fell and hit a pedestrian on corner of Teaneck Road and West Ivy Lane.
In Stamford, 1178 homes were without power due to downed trees and power lines. In Shippan, live wires were down on Harvard Avenue.
Numerous trees and power lines were downed in West Haven, Cheshire, and Guilford.  A downed tree blocked Treadwell Street in Hamden, and 1200 customers were without power.
Debris was blown off a building northwest of Crown Heights Brooklyn due to strong and gusty winds.
Due to strong winds, scaffolding blew off a building at 120 Summit Ave. Residents were evacuated.

Numerous trees were downed due to strong winds.  A tree fell on Portion Road between Morris Ave. and Maple Crest Drive in Farmingville.  A large tree was down at the intersection of Pine St. and Wilson Blvd. in Islip.
Numerous trees were downed near Riverhead due to strong winds.  A large tree was downed on Ackerly Pond Lane in Southold.
A 60 mph peak wind speed was measured at Shinnecock Hills at 151 pm.
More than 150 traffic accidents occurred across Bridgeport, Norwalk, and Stamford Connecticut due to icy road conditions.
Route 107 was completely impassable Thursday morning.  Dozens of traffic accidents occurred in Ridgefield, with a five car crash on Turney Rd. at 730 am.
Dozens of traffic accidents occurred due to slippery roads and several schools closed in Waterbury.
Nearly 90 traffic accidents occurred in a few hours Thursday morning in Wayne, NJ and 75 accidents in Clifton, NJ.  Several injuries occurred due to crashes.
Several dozen traffic accidents were reported Thursday morning due to icy road conditions, mainly from 7 am to 930 am.
A 60 mph wind gust was reported in Atlantic Beach at 1 am on February 26th.

A wind gust to 62 mph was reported at White Plains at 629 pm. In Larchmont, a 58 mph wind gust was reported at 710 pm. A tree fell onto a car, killing one person and injuring another at 645 pm in Hartsdale.
Trees were knocked down and blocked 2 lanes on Highway 303. This occurred at 340 pm.

A gust to 68 mph was reported by a trained spotter at 255 pm.  Another gust to 67 mph was reported by yet another spotter.  A tree fell on a house in Seaford at 315 pm.  In fact, there were numerous reports of trees down from 2 pm through 5 pm.  Approximately 400 trees were downed across the county. A gust to 67 mph was reported in Bayville at 435 pm.
A roof was blown off a building in Rahway at 757 pm due to strong and gusty winds. A wind gust to 55 mph was reported at Caldwell Airport at 605 pm.

A trained spotter reported a wind gust of 66 mph in Fort Lee at 634 pm. Teterboro Airport reported a wind gust to 59 mph at 743 pm.  A tree fell onto multiple cars traping and injuring people.  This occurred at 446 pm in Teaneck.

A wind gust to 58 mph was reported in Westport at 320 pm. At Bridgeport Sikorsky Airport, a wind gust of 60 mph was reported at 430 pm.  The public reported a wind gust to 65 mph in Norwalk at 515 pm. There was widespread trees downed by the storm. Some towns that reported many trees down were Darien and Norwalk. There were 2 deaths due to fallen trees. One woman from Westport was killed. Another woman from Greenwich was killed by a fallen tree.
A wind gust to 65 mph was reported by the public in Coney Island. This wind gust was recorded at 9 pm.  Large trees were knocked down on cars and houses.  Boats in bays were damaged.
A 68 mph wind gust was reported at the Moriches US Coast Guard station at 920 pm.  In Mecox, a 65 mph wind gust was reported at 1120 pm.
A wind gust to 63 mph was reported at Great Gull Island at 956 pm.

A trained spotter reported a wind gust to 60 mph in Lindenhurst at 450 pm.  Other wind gusts reported were 69 mph in Blue Point at 934 pm, 67 mph in Fire Island at 7 pm, 66 mph in Amity Harbor at 621 pm, 64 mph in Patchogue at 710 pm, 62 mph at Islip MacArthur Airport at 636 pm, and 60 mph at Farmingdale Airport at 636 pm. A tree fell and killed a 73 year old woman in Bay Shore as she walked to her car. This occurred on Lanier Lane at 820 pm.
A 59 mph wind gust was reported at the Groton New London Airport at 812 pm.
Numerous trees were downed in Maplewood and South Orange around 1030 am.
A 78 mph wind gust was reported at Robbins Reef at 718 pm.

Heavy wet snow accumulated on trees.  One branch fell on and killed a male in his 30s in Central Park around 3:58 pm EST.  Numerous trees were downed from 69th through 71st streets along 5th Avenue.  One tree fell on and crushed a city bus with people in it.  No injuries were reported.
The Rahway River at Springfield exceeded its flood stage and crested at 5.53 feet.
The Mahwah River at Suffern exceeded bankfull and crested at 4.88 feet.

Water rose to 10.4 ft. MLLW at 924 pm EST at the NOS tidal gage at Bridgeport CT. This is right at the moderate flooding benchmark.  In addition, numerous roads were closed near the shore in Bridgeport on the evening of March 13th.  Paylifters had to remove sand and debris from residences and streets in this area.

The Bayville Causeway to Center Island was blocked by rocks and debris, including a 200 pound concrete rock pushed onto the roadway, by high surf.  Jones Beach suffered major flooding and beach erosion as waves up to 20 feet battered the shore.  It was completely inundated with water through much of the weekend.
The Staten Island ferry was closed for a time due to high surf the evening of March 13th.

The Hamptons suffered the worst beach erosion in 20 years according to Suffolk County officials as waves up to 20 ft battered the shoreline. The Hamptons are estimated to have suffered at least 30 million dollars in property damage.

Robert Moses State Park suffered major flooding and erosion during the March 12 to 15 coastal storm as waves up to 20 feet battered the shoreline. The storm left only 10 feet separating the ocean front from the east end of the boardwalk. State Park officials estimated that the storm washed away more than 100 feet of beach depth at Fields 4 and 5 at Robert Moses. This will require 200,000 cubic feet of sand to be placed on the shore in April at an estimated cost of 1 million dollars.
Huntingtown Town trucks had to dump 1000 tons of crushed stone to bolster a compromised sea wall along the only access road into Asharoken.
Orient Beach State Park sustained moderate to heavy beach erosion the weekend of March 13-14th, with debris washing up onto the road and park.
Route 7 in Kearney was closed in both directions due to tidal flooding on the morning of March 29th.
Dune Road was closed due to high surf in Westhampton during the afternoon and evening of March 29th.

Total rainfall recorded at Belvedere Castle in Central Park was 4.38 inches. In addition, total precipitation for the month of March was 10.69 inches which broke the old record of 10.54 inches set in 1983.

Total precipitation for the month of March was 8.62 inches at JFK Airport which broke the old record of 8.17 inches set in 1980. Widespread basement flooding occurred throughout New Canaan and extending into the Old Bridgeport area.  This was exacerbated by storm surge in the Old Bridgeport area, which caused the closing of Sound Beach Ave. between Lincoln Ave. and Vista Avenue.  Widespread small stream flooding was also reported in New Canaan.||Total rainfall amounts received across Fairfield County ranged from 3.84 inches at Sikorsky Memorial Airport in Bridgeport to 4.78 inches in Shelton.

The Old Saybrook Police Department on Main St. suffered severe flood damage to the building, stored equipment and records after 8 inches of water accumulated in the basement.  The Parks and Recreation Department building also in Old Saybrook and the Senior Center in Westbrook also suffered from minor flood damage.  In Clinton, widespread damage to houses from flooding was reported across town.
Cars were stuck in water covering Centennial Ave. in Meriden.  Many basements were also flooded throughout the town of Meriden.

A mudslide at the Newfield St. apartment complex in Middletown left the concrete foundation of one of the buildings exposed with a sheer drop to the Coginchaug River below.||Total rainfall amounts received across Middlesex County ranged from 5.14 inches in Portland to 5.67 inches in Clinton.

Long Hill Rd. in Guilford was closed with moderate flooding occurring. In Stonington and N. Stonington, numerous roads were closed and reports of numerous houses with serious basement flooding, up to 3 ft. high, was received.  The intersection of Montauk Ave. and Mistuxet Ave. just outside of Mystic was also closed due to flooding.  Several basement offices in Stonington Town Hall on Elm St. were flooded.  Floodwaters also caused extensive damage to the bridge over Shunock Brook on Wyassup Rd. between Avery Ln. and Main St., and a historic 150 year old building that houses the Watermark Cafe and the Village Hardware Store.  Lantern Hill Rd, Grindstone Hill Rd., Loin Hill Rd. and Pinewoods Rd. were completely washed out and in need of major repairs.
In Groton, many streams were above bankfull and numerous homes experienced basement flooding.

In Groton, Route 117 between US-1 and Groton Public Library located at 52 Newtown Rd. was closed due to flooding. In Old Mystic, Route 27 was closed at the Groton-Stonington town line due to flooding with water rescues being performed by Old Mystic Fire Dept.

Routes 32 and 163 in Montville were closed in both directions due to flooding.  Several water rescues were performed on Maple Ave. also in Montville as well as on I-395 in Norwich and various roads in Salem.
A bridge on Shewville Rd. in Groton was washed out.

In Old Mystic, raging waters from a small stream that empties into the Mystic River tore out a small bridge on Route 184, flooded numerous homes and businesses, such as the Old Mystic General Store, post office and Old Mystic Mill on Main St., as well as trapped cars. Route 27 nearby remained closed and River Rd. was eventually closed as well.||Total rainfall amounts received across New London County ranged from 6.04 in Old Lyme to 8.60 in Mystic.

The Pawcatuck River Bridge located on W. Broad St. and the Stillman Ave. Bridge over the Pawcatuck River were closed due to the concern that debris in the raging waters pounding the side of the roadways were damaging the integity and stability of the bridges.  Several businesses along the river experienced damage due to flooding.

In Stonington, a bridge on Greenhaven Rd. between Palmer Neck Rd. and Route 1 that spans over what is usually a small creek that flows into the Wequetequock Cove was destroyed by flood waters.  A large section of the road was also washed away and several nearby homes were flooded.

Numerous roads were closed in Mystic and Pawcatuck due to flooding. In the Birdland neighborhood of Pawcatuck, Route 1 was closed from Spellman Dr. to S. Anguilla Rd.  Residents on Milan Terrance experienced basement flooding.  In Mystic, Route 1 was closed near Bishop's Cove. Portions of Pequot Trail, Jerry Brown Rd. near the Aquarion Water Co. and Coogan Blvd were also closed.  A small bridge on Collins Rd. was also badly damaged from flooding.

Major flooding occurred on the Yantic River at Yantic.  The river crested at 13.23 ft. on March 30, 2010 at 1600 EST.  As a result, West Town St. was closed at several intersections, including Case St., Sholes Ave. and at I-395. Sections of the New London Turnpike were closed as was the Canada Bridge on Sherman Rd.  The Yantic Voulnteer Fire Dept. on Yantic Rd. sustained damage due to flood waters.

Major flooding occurred on the Quinnebaug River at Jewett City.  The river crested at 23.26 ft. at 0630 EST on March 31, 2010 and remained above flood stage until the morning of April 1.  As a result, roads were damaged by flood waters including, South Main St. A retaining wall was also damaged on School St.  A woman nearly electrocuted herself while attempting to unplug a clothes dryer.  Water inside the walls of her 24 Wedgewood Dr. apartment caused the wire to become live and she was badly shocked and taken to the hospital.  Coincidentally, 13 other apartments were evacuated after the ceilings collapsed inside the first and second-floor apartments.  The Jewett City sewage treatment plant also located on Wedgewood Dr. suffered severe flooding and the National Guard was called in to assist in the efforts to keep raw sewage from backing into homes and into the Quinebaug River.
In Ledyard, Lambtown Road Extension was closed due to flooding.

In the Griswold neighborhood of Jewett City, many roads were damaged by flood waters, including Sheldon Rd., Campbell Rd., Bitgood Rd., Coal Pit Hill Rd., Popple Bridge Rd., Colonel Brown Rd. and Geer Rd.  A house sustained damage on Pachaug Pond. and a bridge on Sheldon Rd. was closed because of damage.

Super saturated grounds caused a 70 ft. tree to fall on a house on Great Plains Rd in Danbury.  Another tree fell on a house on Hudson Dr. in New Fairfield, taking down the utility wires from the road to the home.  The sewer system backed up into the Bethel Police Dept. on Plumtrees Rd. and was inundated by a mix of rain water and raw sewage.
In Stamford, many basements were flooded on Cedar Heights Rd. and in the Shippan Point area.

Many basements and roads were flooded in Aquebogue, Southold, Riverhead and Wading River.
The Quinebaug River fell to moderate flooding around midnight on April 1 and continued to recede, falling below its flood stage of 17.5 ft during the morning.
Numerous trees were downed across the area. A large tree fell onto a house at 575 Bunker Hill Ave in Waterbury.

The Ramapo River at Mahwah exceeded bankfull and crested at 11.90 feet at 0500 EST on March 14, just below it's major flooding threshold of 12.0 ft.

Major flooding on the Passaic River caused evacuations of hundreds of residents in the town of Wayne.  Some refused to leave and eventually needed to be rescued by boat.  Severe flooding occurred in numerous homes and businesses close to the river which crested on March 16. Numerous roads and bridges were also closed for several days, including major highways such as Route 46 and Route 23.  The neighborhood of Hoffman Grove and the Hobson Ave. area were still inundated with water on March 18th.

Major flooding on the Passaic River caused evacuations of hundreds of residents in the towns of Totowa and Little Falls.  Dozens refused to leave and eventually needed to be rescued by boat.  Severe flooding occurred in numerous homes and businesses close to the river which crested on March 16.  Numerous roads and bridges were also closed for several days.  More than 800 homes and businesses incurred damage in Totowa.  The property damage amount listed is estimated.

Major flooding on the Passaic River caused evacuations of hundreds of residents in the towns of Paterson and Hawthorne.  Some people refused to leave and eventually needed to be rescued by boat. Fifty-five homes were flooded in Pompton Lakes from the Wanaque, Pequannock and Ramapo Rivers exceeding bankfull.  More than 200 residents had to be rescued by local firefighters in the southern end of town, which is surrounded by the 3 rivers.
Several rivers and small streams exceeded bankfull causing flooding of roads and damage to nearly 5000 homes, 20 of which were condemned.  The property damage amount listed is estimated.

Several dozen trees and power lines were reported down in Great Neck, with several trees uprooted. A NWS Storm Survey found an area of damage that extended over a broad area extending from Old Pond Road east to Hampshire Road, with downed trees facing south and east in those areas respectively in a fanned-out fashion indicative of a microburst. The most severe damage in this swath was concentrated along Old Pond and Strathmore Roads, with dozens of healthy hardwood and pine trees uprooted or snapped in two. This damage is indicative of maximum winds of 100 mph. The path length and maximum path width of the microburst were 0.75 miles. Some of the trees fell onto houses and cars.

An NWS Storm Survey determined that an EF-1 Tornado, with maximum winds of 110 mph, impacted a small portion of Bridgeport. The survey found many signs of wind rotation in a highly localized area just north of Interstate 95. The area was bounded by the Interstate 95 northbound connector on the west and Pembroke Street on the east. The most severe damage was concentrated along East Main Street between Nichols Street on the south and Cedar Street on the North. In this area, windows were blown in, the facade of a building was stripped off, tree tops were sheared off, and large pieces of metal blown off from surrounding structures were wrapped around a fire hydrant. Eyewitness reports described a rain wrapped tornado with visibility near zero in swirling heavy rain and debris. Note the damage estimate is just a portion of the total damage to Bridgeport.

At approximately 1230 pm on June 22nd the motionless body of 12 year old Nicole Suriel was pulled out of the ocean waters. This was more than 90 minutes after she went under the water near a jetty adjacent to Edwards Blvd in Long Beach. Nicole was on a field trip with her Harlem classmates. One of her teachers was injured in attempts to rescue her, ultimately having to be rescued herself. There were no lifeguards officially on duty, with staffing planned to begin the following week,  but dozens of lifeguards and local police who were on nearby training exercises did join in the search efforts.||Robert Moses and Jones Beach reported wave heights of 1/2 to 1 ft in the morning with none to slight rip conditions. Permanent rip currents are likely in the vicinity of fixed structures such as piers and jetties, making them very dangerous bathing locations for inexperienced swimmers.

Shortly after 7 pm on Tuesday June 29th, 14 yr old Scott McLeish of Flatlands was swept to sea by a rip current. His body was not recovered. The incident happened after life guards went off duty, and boy was not a strong swimmer.||Strong rip currents were reported at Jones Beach and  Robert Moses, with dangerous rip currents at  Hither Hills.

Straight line winds in Bridgeport, in addition to the small EF1 Tornado, caused the collapse of 5 complete buildings, including one on Knowlton Street, with damage to 9 other buildings. The winds, estimated at 100 mph also blew a billboard off an apartment building, blew out windows and off bricks from buildings, flipped over a tractor trailer on I-95 between exits 27 and 28, flipped over cars on Route 25 between exits 3 and 4, and tore some siding of off the City Hall Annex. It also tore down radio towers, brought down hundreds of trees, including 2 on a house on Bond Street, and across Route 25 between exits 3 and 4. 57 streets were at least partially closed due to the wind damage. Around two dozen people were displaced by the storm.  Note damage estimate includes damage from the tornado, as the total is hard to separate.

Debris from the damaged hangar and terminal building caused minor damage to an adjacent bar.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey team, along with officials from Portland Emergency Management, found damage consistent with microburst winds up to 110 mph along a swath approximately 2 miles long. The damage swath began near the intersection of State Route 66 and Middle Haddam Road in Portland and ended about 2 miles to the east at Keighly Pond Road in the town of East Hampton. The damage path was approximately 0.5 miles wide at its eastern edge and 1.5 miles wide at its western edge, indicative of divergent winds.||Significant damage to many large, mainly hardwood, trees was observed throughout the damage path, with trees averaging 80 feet in height and up to 2 feet in diameter snapped, in almost all cases, 20 to 30 feet above the ground. This is indicative of wind speeds of 90 to 110 mph.||Most of the damage was observed generally along Middle Haddam Road, with trees mostly oriented directly east or east-southeast. To the north, along Breezy Corners Road and Jobs Pond Road, tree damage was oriented east or east-northeast. To the south, along Lyman Lane and Wellwyn Road, trees were oriented to the southeast. This pattern also indicated diverging winds.||Damage to structures was confined to those in open areas away from trees. One such building, a Farm Center on Middle Haddam Road had a large section of roof ripped off that was carried by the wind for about 100 yards. Other buildings in open areas received minor damage to windows and screens.
Two house fires were caused by lightning strikes.

Southerly winds and long period ocean swells produced dangerous rip currents on Sunday August 8th along the south shores of Suffolk and Nassau Counties. Surf observations from Suffolk County beaches reported moderate rip currents, with a few reports of occasionally strong rip currents. ||There was a fatality due to drowning at Amagansett Beach when a female swimmer was caught in rough surf/rip current.  Local media reported that other swimmers were caught in rip currents as they tried to save the woman, but other injury reports are unconfirmed.||A moderate risk of rip currents was issued in the surf zone forecast. This was also headlined in the Hazardous Weather Outlook issued Saturday evening and Sunday Morning. In addition, the Area Forecast Discussion issued Sunday morning indicated that periods of stronger rip currents were possible.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey Team confirmed a tornado near Park Slope in Brooklyn.||In the northern portion of Prospect Park, there were signs of tree damage that converged towards a well defined narrow path.  Tree tops were twisted and sheared off.  The location of the tornado was bounded by Prospect Park on the west, Flatbush Avenue on the east and Subway Grand Army Plaza to the north.  The tornado formed just southwest of the Brooklyn Public Library and lifted around 2 miles northeast of Park Slope.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey Team confirmed a tornado in Queens.||The tornado impacted Flushing and Bayside.  In Flushing, on Browne Street between Roosevelt and 38th Avenues, the third floor of a residential brick building was severely damaged structurally.  Large tree tops were lying on top of buildings and shot like projectiles between buildings.  Sides of houses were peeled back.  There was clear evidence of twisted metal along the side of the building.  On Warren Street near the intersection of Roosevelt Avenue, a steel framed water tower was blown over on the roof.  There was a partial roof collapse on another residential building.||A Pennsylvania woman was killed in her car by a falling tree on Grand Central Parkway.  Her passenger was injured.  A man trying to assist the woman suffered a brain aneurysm and died. ||The tornado touched down around 2.5 miles south of Flushing and lifted 1 mile northeast of Bayside over Little Neck Bay.
A deliveryman was injured at 7th Avenue and 9th Street as plate-glass windows were blown out of the Brooklyn Industries Store.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey verified the occurance of a macroburst in Queens.  The path extended from Middle Village east across Forest Hills.||In Forest Hills, at MacDonald Park, a field of trees were sheared off which completely demolished the park.  Many whole trees and large branches were downed in a divergent pattern.  This was a clear signature of macroburst wind damage.||The area of the macroburst was bounded by Queens Boulevard and 69th Road to the northeast near the intersection of Yellowstone Boulevard.||Just southwest of the Long Island Expressway along 63rd Avenue and near the intersections of Reeves Avenue and 146th Street, many huge healthy 36 inch diameter trees fell in nearly the same direction in narrow roads.  Downed trees destroyed many cars and made entries to houses impassable.  Widespread tree damage made many secondary and tertiary roads impassable.||Many whole trees and large branches were downed near Queens College, along Dartmouth Street and in Forest Hills Garden, and along Park Drive East in Kew Garden Hills.

Numerous roads were closed due to flooding in the towns of New Haven and West Haven.  A school bus loaded with children became stuck in high water at the intersection of Washington Ave. and Wood St. in West Haven.  The water was so high that the children had to stand on the seats to avoid getting wet.  The local fire department rescued the children on board.  The basement of Seth Haley School on South St. in West Haven filled with two to three feet of water in approximately ten minutes and caused the school to be closed for the day.  Rainfall totals ranged from 1.73 inches at New Haven/Tweed Airport to 3.05 inches in Hamden.

In Wilton, a man and a woman drowned shortly after launching their 2-person kayak into the swollen Norwalk River in the early evening hours after the heavy rain had ceased.  Neither of them were wearing a life preserver, and the river was moving quickly at the time of the accident.  Rainfall totals ranged from 1.59 inches in Bridgeport to 5.54 inches in Danbury.
The intersection of Route 136 and South Main Street in Norwalk was under several feet of water.

Some minor coastal flooding was reported in the area of Rockaway Boulevard and Brookville Boulevard near John F. Kennedy International Airport, as a few vehicles were stuck in flood waters between 5:30 pm and 6:00 pm (EDT).  Three calls were placed to 911 for assistance.  No injuries were reported and the coastal flooding resulted in a temporary road closure until the waters receded.

The USGS gauge at Freeport exceeded its moderate flood stage of 5.8 feet MLLW at 5:00 pm (EDT), peaking at 6.14 feet MLLW at 5:42 pm (EDT).  During this time, significant street flooding was observed on Hudson Avenue in Freeport.
Ponding of water six inches deep accumulated alongside a major swamp located near the intersection of Boggs Hill Rd. and Palestine Rd in Newtown.
Sections of Route 25 in Monroe and off Exit 33 of Interstate 95 in Stratford were closed due to flooding.

Flooding caused portions of many major roads to be closed.  Specifically, the Saw Mill River Parkway was closed in both directions between the Taconic State Pkwy. and Manville Rd. in Pleasantville. The Bronx River Pkwy. was shut in both directions from the Sprain Brook Pkwy. in Yonkers to the Main St. Bridge in White Plains.  Fourteen families living in a two-story apartment building on Harrison Ave. in Harrison were evacuated after a ceiling in the hallway collapsed, causing flooding throughout the building.  Property damage amounts are estimated.  Total rainfall amounts ranged from 3.58 inches in White Plains to 6.25 inches in Yorktown Heights.

The stream off of Route 118 overflowed its banks washing away the front yard of one resident and inundated the garage and basement of another homeowner on Lakeview Dr. in Somers.  Property damage amount is estimated.

Two to three feet of standing water accumulated on the roads in North Arlington.
Several inches of water was rushing down Eighth St. and entering some residences in Park Slope.

Downed telephone poles were reported on Route 22 West in Union due to strong winds Sunday night, December 27th.

Strong winds blew roofing material off a warehouse on the 2900 Block of Richmond Terrace in Mariner's Harbor, striking nearby power cables and resulting in the streets closure between Union and Dehart Avenues Sunday night, December 27th. Strong winds and whiteout conditions forced the closure of the lower level of the Verrazano Narrows Bridge Sunday night as well.
An Oceanside man died of a heart attack while shoveling snow Monday, December 27th.

Approximately 15 road closures were reported Sunday night into Monday, December 27th, due to downed trees and power lines fully or partially blocking the roadways around Wilton, with over 1100 people without power in the town. Tuesday afternoon a 20 foot section of roof collapsed at Lawn Doctor's production facility on Viaduct Road in Stamford, but no one was injured.

The strong winds caused a large gas station canopy to collapse on Washington Avenue in North Haven and a tree to fall in Hamden between midnight and 1 am EST Sunday night, December 27th. Meanwhile in Wallingford, an 80 foot spruce tree was toppled onto a house on Pond Hill Road Sunday night.

The strong winds downed trees and power lines on Jamestown Drive in Guilford Sunday night, December 27th. In Madison, a large tree crashed through the roof of a house around 330 am EST Sunday night on Woodlawn Avenue.
About 50 residents around Pond Meadow Road in Westbrook lost power after a large tree fell across a power line at 11 pm on Sunday night, December 27th.

The strong winds blew out 900 pounds of storefront glass at Abbey Carpet in New London Shopping Center in New London Sunday night, December 27th, while at the Garde Arts Center several awnings were shredded or ripped off the building.
Downed trees on power lines caused a major power outage Tuesday morning, December 28th, in Stonington, with 2745 customers without power for a while as a result.

High surf and high tides caused flooding of roads and damage to a multi-million dollar home in Montauk's Soundview section Sunday night December 27th, with the beach stairs gone, the lower decks ripped away, and the entire foundation compromised. Storm surge also ripped away bulkheads in front of homes along Captain Kidd's Path, with the Montauk Bell Buoy washing at the end of the path. In addition, moderate beach erosion was reported at Montauk area parks.

High surf and high tides Sunday Night December 27th caused flooding of roads and damage to two homes on the North Fork. The two homes are located at Hashamomuck Cove in Southhold. The bulkhead of one of the homes was completely destroyed and the cellar gone. The storm also flooded two thirds of Orient Beach State Park and caused signifcant erosion along the Gardiner's bay Shoreline. Further west the erosion undermined the shoulder of Soundview Avenue.

A Mastic Beach woman was struck and killed on Wednesday 1/26 by a pickup truck plowing a Center Moriches bus company parking lot.

Three barns collapsed on the morning of January 19th in Newtown due to the weight of accumulated heavy snow. A barn on 57 West Street in Newtown collapsed at around 9:49 am. Another barn collapsed around 8:30 am that morning at the intersection of Currituck Road and Hedge Meadow Lane, while a third barn collapsed around the same time on the intersection of Currituck Road and Butterfield Road.
The roof of a vacant building at 1198 New Haven Road in Naugatuck collapsed under the weight of heavy accumulated snow.

Runoff from heavy rain caused basement flooding in the town of Yorktown Heights.

High water levels caused flooding on the bridge which was closed to traffic and inhibited access into and out of certain parts of town.||The river gauge on the Ramapo River at Ramapo, which is downstream of the aforementioned location, crested at 10.7 feet at 8:45 am on March 7.
Moodna Creek overflowed its banks causing flooding of first floor residents and businesses on Route 208 as well as Route 94 near Washingtonville High School.

The Still River exceeded bankfull causing Rt. 6 and Newtown Rd. to be closed.

In addition, a partial collapse to a roof of a building at 1701 Highland Ave. and the rear of a 136 yr. old George Keeler Stove Shop at 166 S. Main Street occurred Wednesday morning.||A building at 505 Main St. in Middletown collapsed on the morning of February 2nd after the roof and 3rd floor caved in due the excessive weight of snow and ice.||A storage barn at 91 Library Road in Southbury came crashing down early Wednesday afternoon under the weight of snow and ice.
A manufacturing building on Woodmont Road in Milford was destroyed Wednesday morning around 1105 am, when wooden support trusses under the flat roof failed under the weight of heavy snow and ice.
In Hebron, the roof of a ranch style house on West Street collapsed on Wednesday morning pushing out the structures walls and crushing a car in the garage.

A barn roof collapsed in Bethany at around 4 pm Wednesday afternoon February 2nd at the end of a cul-de-sac on Hunter Trail.  The weight of the snow and ice caused the roof to pancake and trap between 12 and 15 horses.  Rescue operations took 3 1/2 hours.  Also in Bethany, about 13 people escaped injury Wednesday afternoon when half of the roof collapsed at Fairfield County Millwork Inc., at 20 Sargent Drive. ||In Naugatuck, part of the roof at Thurston Energy at 410 Rubber Avenue, collapsed Thursday morning February 3rd under the weight of snow and ice.  The garage of a vacant house on the corner of Arch and Scott streets collapsed as well on Thursday. Mayor Robert A. Mezzo of Naugatuck declared a state of emergency Friday February 4th as a result of widespread structural damage to buildings across the borough due to heavy snow and ice loads.||In Wolcott, a garage at 1615 Meriden Road, used as storage for several aging school buses collapsed on Thursday around 1:30 pm.||In Meriden, the roof of a detached 3 car garage on 599 North Colony Street collapsed under the weight of snow and ice on Friday evening.
A vacant Willard Road building in Norwalk experienced a partial roof collapse due to heavy snow and ice Thursday afternoon February 3rd.

The weight of heavy snow and ice caused about 200 feet of a wall to collapse at the state armory building in New Haven, Monday Night February 7th.  The incident occurred around 6:30 pm.
A real estate agency collapsed Tuesday morning, February 8th on Route 101 in Norwich due to the heavy weight of snow and ice.

The roof of three connected garages at the Bradford Arms Apartments on East Bradford Avenue in Verona collapsed under the weight of snow and ice on Saturday February 5th. Two unoccupied vehicles were heavily damaged as a result of the collapse.
Eighty four year old Ada Eads was found dead of hypothermia or exposure to the cold weather on High Point Road in Westport Connecticut on Thursday morning around 8:00 am by trash collectors.

Based on a storm survey performed by the National Weather Service, radar signatures, and eyewitness reports, the National Weather Service confirmed an EF-1 tornado that ran from Goshen to Blooming Grove NY, on Friday July 29th.|The tornado touched down near 109 Coleman Road and lifted near 600 Craigsville Road in Goshen, then skipped along near Craigsville Road, before finally lifting near 379 Prospect Road in Blooming Grove.  All along this path, trees converged into a well-defined narrow path. The most significant property damage occurred on Hasbrouck Road in Goshen, where 2 houses directly across the street from one another - 101 and 110 Hasbrouck - were impacted.  At 101 Hasbrouck Road, roof shingles were torn off, skylight windows were blown in with glass shattering, and debris was embedded all along the sides of the house including a small branch that went right through a gutter.  At 110 Hasbrouck Road, trees were draped all over the house with minor structural damage.
A funnel cloud was reported near the intersection of Railroad Avenue and Route 9W near West Haverstraw.

A storm survey team consisting of meteorologists from the National Weather Service and staff from the Westchester Office of Emergency Management conducted a ground and aerial survey of wind damage from thunderstorms on Friday July 29th. Based on information gathered during the survey and conversations with local residences, the damage is being attributed to a microburst.  The microburst had estimated maximum gusts of 80 mph associated with it, a path length of about 1.4 miles, and a maximum path width of 0.4 miles.||Damage from this microburst began on the Croton River along Route 9 and spread south-southeast towards central Ossining.  The damage consisted primarily of snapped trees.  A large 3-4 foot diameter tree fell on Route 9 near Eagle Bay Drive taking down power lines that resulted in the snapping of several telephone poles.  Significant tree damage occurred at Cedar Lane Terrace at 6 Meadowbrook Drive. The tree damage was noted in a divergent pattern.

A raft carrying five men capsized on the Croton River just south of Silver Lake Park shortly before 6 pm.  The men were rescued from the raging river, which was moving at a speed of around 40 mph, but not before three of the rescue workers were tossed from their rescue boat and were swept under a trestle bridge just south of the Croton-Harmon station. This is the second of four segments of a combined waterspout tornado event. The tornado originated as a waterspout approximately 1 mile south of the tip of Breezy Point at 10:56 am in ANZ-355, and crossed onto land, as a tornado approximately 2500 feet northeast of the tip of Breezy Point, Queens at 10:58 am. The tornado caused structural damage to the Breezy Point Surf Club near where the waterspout came onshore as a tornado. Damage was also reported near its exit point off Breezy Point, with multiple trees and power lines reported down near the Beach 216th Street, at 10:59 am. At this point the tornado exited as a waterspout into the eastern arm of Lower New York Harbor, ANZ-338, about 12,500 feet west of Rockaway Inlet. The waterspout then continued northeast until making landfall as a tornado in Kings County/Brooklyn to the southeast of Plumb Beach about 750 feet south of the Belt Parkway at 11:01 am. The tornado then continued moving northeast into Brooklyn where it produced EF1 damage in Canarsie, Brooklyn before lifting at 11:05 am.

This is the fourth segment of a combined waterspout/tornado that originated as a waterspout about 1 mile south of the tip of Breezy Point in ANZ-355 (Coastal Waters From Sandy Hook NJ to Fire Island Inlet NY out to 20 Nautical Miles) at 10:56 am.  The waterspout then reached land and crossed Breezy Point Queens as an EF0 tornado from 10:58 to 10:59 am. The tornado then went back over water, traversing the Eastern Arm of Lower New York Harbor (ANZ-338), to the west of Rockaway Inlet, from 10:59-11:00 am as a waterspout. At 11:01 am, the waterspout made landfall as a tornado to the southeast of Plumb Beach, about 750 feet south of the Belt Parkway. The tornado traversed northeast across Marine Park, based on video evidence, then through the Mill Basin Section of Kings County/Brooklyn where it brought down a tree and limbs along Whitman Drive around 11:02 am. The tornado continued heading northeast into Bergen Beach where it downed a tree and several limbs between the corner of East 70th Street and Avenue Y and the corner of Royce Street and Avenue W around 11:03 am. The tornado then crossed the Canarsie section of Kings County/Brooklyn from 11:04 to 11:05 am before lifting near the corner of East 94th Street and Avenue N. In Canarsie, the tornado caused structural damage to several homes and to several trees in and around Canarsie Park.

events.event_narrative: This is the first segment in a four segment combined waterspout and tornado event. Based on eyewitness accounts and video evidence a waterspout formed about 1 mile south of the tip of Breezy Point around 10:56 am and moved northeast, making landfall about 2500 feet northeast of the tip of Breezy Point, Queens, near the Breezy Point Surf Club, around 10:58 am. The storm then crossed Breezy Point Queens as an EF0 tornado from 10:58 to 10:59 am, before reemerging into the eastern arm of Lower New York Harbor approximately 12500 feet west of Rockaway Inlet. The waterspout then moved northeast and crossed land to the southeast of Plumb Beach in Kings County/Brooklyn about 11:02 am. The EF1 tornado continued northeast to Canarsie, Brooklyn where it lifted at 11:05 am.

This is the third segment in a four segment combined waterspout and tornado event. The storm originated as a waterspout about 1 mile south of the tip of Breezy Point around 10:56 am and moved northeast, making landfall about 2500 feet northeast of the tip of Breezy Point, Queens, near the Breezy Point Surf Club, around 10:58 am. The storm then crossed Breezy Point Queens as an EF0 tornado from 10:58 to 10:59 am, before reemerging into the eastern arm of Lower New York Harbor approximately 12500 feet west of Rockaway Inlet. Based on photographic and video evidence showing a waterspout near the southwest and northeast points of the track, and no radar evidence of weakening of the circulation, there is no reason to believe the waterspout was not continuous as it traversed the New York Harbor from 10:59 to 11:01 am. The waterspout then crossed land to the southeast of Plumb Beach in Kings County/Brooklyn about 11:01 am. The EF1 tornado continued northeast to Canarsie, Brooklyn where it lifted at 11:05 am.

Southern, Eastern and Western portions of Manhattan experienced two successive tidal cycles with at least moderate coastal flooding. The peak of this surge occurred Monday Night as Sandy made landfall in Southern New Jersey, with widespread record coastal flooding occurring in Lower New York Harbor exceeding the FEMA 100 year base flood elevations. Peak storm tides surpassed all previously documented high water marks, including the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peaks from Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Donna in 1960.||The record storm tide levels along the south shore of New York City resulted from a peak storm surge of about 8 to 10 feet that coincided with normal high tides. These storm tides resulted in up to 3 to 6 feet of inundation along the south shore of Manhattan, with up to 2 to 4 feet of inundation along the East River and Hudson River neighborhoods.||Two fatalities were attributed to the storm surge in Manhattan.

Widespread moderate to major coastal flooding occurred along Newark Bay and the Arthur Kill as peak storm tides in New York Harbor surpassed all previously documented high water marks, including the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peak surge from Hurricane Irene in 2011.||Up to 3 to 6 feet of inundation was experienced in the Chemical Coast along the Arthur Kill and in the Elizabeth Port Authority Marine Terminal along Newark Bay. The inundation generally extended about 2 miles inland past the New Jersey Turnpike, while a few feet of inundation occurred 5 miles inland on the Rahway River. ||This inundation caused areas of moderate to major damage to industrial complexes, such as the Bayway refinery. In addition, the Elizabeth Port System was disrupted for a week to repair road and rail ways, hundreds of displaced shipping containers, damaged electrical systems and other port cargo from the inundation. Also, over 10,000 cars were destroyed in the Elizabeth and Newark Port System from the salt water inundation. ||The marina in the port area of Elizabeth, N.J. was destroyed in the tidal surge in Monday's overnight hours, according to Union County, N.J. spokesman Sebastian D���Elia. He said the marina was ���pretty much gone��� and that the boats were scattered, along with the surrounding neighborhood sustaining damage.||Flooding from the tidal surge also impacted 20-30 homes in the Trembly Point neighborhood of Linden, N.J., according to Union County spokesman Sebastian D'Elia.

Widespread record coastal flooding occurred in Lower New York Harbor exceeding the FEMA 100 year base flood elevations.  Peak storm tides surpassed all previously documented high water marks, including the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peaks from Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Donna in 1960.||The record storm tide levels along the Eastern Shore of Staten Island resulted from a peak storm surge of about 9 to 11 feet that coincided with normal high tides. These storm tides in conjunction with several feet of wave action resulted in up to 5 to 8 feet of inundation along the northeast coast of Staten Island. Townships such as South Beach, Midland Beach, New Dorp, Oakwood Beach, and Great Kills sustained widespread major property damage and loss of life.||Up to 4 to 6 feet of inundation was experienced across the southeast tip of Staten Island, with 2 to 6 feet of inundation along the Arthur Kill in Western Staten Island.||Twenty three fatalities were directly attributed to the storm surge and high surf in Staten Island.

Coastal communities along the Bronx experienced two successive tidal cycles with at least moderate coastal flooding. The peak of this surge occurred Monday Night as Sandy made landfall in Southern New Jersey, with widespread major coastal flooding occurring along Western Long Island Sound. Peak storm tides surpassed water levels from the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peaks from Hurricane Irene in 2011. The major storm tide levels in Western Long Island Sound resulted from a peak storm surge of about 8 to 10 feet that coincided with normal high tides. ||These storm tides resulted in up to 2 to 4 feet of inundation several blocks inland along Long Island Sound, East River and Harlem River and in adjacent communities in areas such as Harding Park, Port Morris, Mott Haven, Locust Point, Clason Point, City Island and Edgewater Park. Two or more Harding Park homes were condemned and a handful of Edgewater Park homes were completely destroyed. Flood waters also surged in Mott Haven late Monday, inundating the intersection of Bruckner Blvd. and Alexander Ave. for several hours. Warehouses and monuments in Port Morris suffered water damage.

Coastal communities along Southern Brooklyn experienced two successive tidal cycles with at least moderate coastal flooding. The peak of this surge occurred Monday Night as Sandy made landfall in Southern New Jersey, with widespread record coastal flooding occurring along New York Harbor and Jamaica Bay exceeding the FEMA 100 year base flood elevations. Peak storm tides surpassed all previously documented high water marks, including the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peaks from Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Donna in 1960. ||The storm tide levels along the Brooklyn shores resulted from a peak storm surge of about 7 to 10 feet that coincided with normal high tides. These storm tides resulted in up to 3 to 5 feet of inundation along the northeastern and southern coasts of Brooklyn.||The hardest hit area in Northeast Brooklyn was Red Hook getting inundated from Upper New York Bay. Additionally, other areas hard hit were Greenpoint and Williamsburg from inundation of Newtown Creek; and Brooklyn Heights from inundation of the East River and Upper New York Bay. ||In southwest Brooklyn; the shoreline communities including Sea Gate, Coney Island, and Manhattan Beach, experienced significant inundation from storm tide and wave action. Numerous homes in this area experienced major structural damage. Inundation extended inland to Avenue X into Bensonhurst, Gravesend and Sheepshead Bay, shutting down the Belt Parkway.||In southeast Brooklyn, the hardest hit areas were Gerritsen Beach, Floyd Bennet, Bergen Beach, Mill Basin, and Canarsie due to inundation from Jamaica Bay and Rockaway Inlet several blocks inland.||Five fatalities were directly attributed to the surge in Brooklyn.

Coastal communities along Southern Queens experienced two successive tidal cycles with at least moderate coastal flooding. The peak of this surge occurred Monday Night as Sandy made landfall in Southern New Jersey, with widespread record coastal flooding occurring along Jamaica Bay exceeding the FEMA 100 year base flood elevations. Peak storm tides surpassed all previously documented high water marks, including the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peaks from Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Donna in 1960.||The storm tide levels along the Queens shores resulted from a peak storm surge of about 7 to 9 feet that coincided with normal high tides. This resulted in up to 3 to 5 feet of inundation of communities in and along Jamaica Bay. Inundation several blocks inland was experienced across coastal communities such as Howard Beach, Brookville and Inwood. Widespread major residential damage was experienced across areas such as Broad Channel, Meadowmere Park, and Old Howard Beach, where some of the deeper inundation occurred. In addition, JFK Airport experienced 1 to 3 feet of inundation onto portions of their runways.||Across the Rockaways, up to 4 and 7 feet of inundation occurred over the peninsula due to surge from Jamaica Bay on the north side and from surge and wave action from the Atlantic Ocean on the south side. Widespread major damage was experienced across the entire length of the Rockaways, with numerous homes and businesses in Breezy Point, Arverne-Edgemere and Seaside experiencing complete destruction. Atlantic Ocean facing shoreline structures, such as boardwalks and several oceanfront homes were destroyed due to runup and setup on top of storm tide from high wave action of at least 10 to 15 feet from the Atlantic Ocean.||Six fatalities were directly attributed to the storm surge and high surf in Queens.

Coastal communities along Northern Queens experienced two successive tidal cycles  with at least moderate coastal flooding. The peak of this surge occurred Monday Night as Sandy made landfall in Southern New Jersey, with widespread major coastal flooding occurring along Western Long Island Sound. Peak storm tides surpassed water levels from the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peaks from Hurricane Irene in 2011. The storm tide levels in Western Long Island Sound resulted from a peak storm surge of about 8 to 10 feet that coincided with normal high tides.||These storm tides resulted in up to 3 to 6 feet of inundation within a few blocks of the East River and Newtown Creek in Hunters Point as well as Astoria along the East River. ||Additionally, 2 to 4 feet of inundation was observed over runway 13 and the northern portion of runway 22 at LaGuardia Airport, with water making it all the way to the terminal building.

Coastal communities along Southwest Suffolk County experienced four successive tidal cycles with at least moderate coastal flooding, with 3 of those tidal cycles well above major flood thresholds. The peak of this surge occurred Monday Night as Sandy made landfall in Southern New Jersey, with widespread record coastal flooding occurring along the Great South Bay exceeding the FEMA 100 to 500 year base flood elevations. Peak storm tides surpassed all previously documented high water marks, including the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peaks from Hurricane Irene in 2011.||The storm tide levels along the Southwest Suffolk County shore resulted from a peak storm surge of about 6 to 7 feet that coincided with normal high tides. This resulted in up to 2 to 5 feet of inundation of communities in and along Great South Bay. The majority of locations south of Montauk Highway from Amityville to Islip were completely inundated, with areas east to Brookhaven inundated several blocks inward from the shoreline.  Areas of major residential damage were experienced across low lying areas such as Amityville, Lindenhurst, and Babylon.||The most widespread major damage was experienced along the barrier beach communities, where the surge was amplified by the runup and setup from 15 to 20 foot breakers along the Atlantic Ocean coast. On Fire Island, up to 30 ocean front homes and other ocean facing structures, such as boardwalks and piers, were completely destroyed by the storm tide and battering waves. A full breach of the barrier island also occurred just west of the Smith Point Bridge on Fire Island. In Robert Moses State Park, partial roadway collapses occurred along the south side of water tower and eastbound park road. Severe erosion occurred throughout the park as well as extensive boardwalk damage.

Coastal communities along Northern Nassau County experienced two successive tidal cycles with at least moderate coastal flooding. The peak of this surge occurred Monday Night as Sandy made landfall in Southern New Jersey, with widespread major coastal flooding occurring along Western Long Island Sound. ||Peak storm tides surpassed water levels from the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peak surges from Hurricane Irene in 2011. Repeated attempts to reach the men failed before firefighters were able to surmount the high water in a sanitation department dump truck.

Low lying areas along the Hudson River experienced moderate coastal flooding as storm surge moved north along the river Monday Night as Sandy made landfall in Southern New Jersey. This coincided with widespread record coastal flooding occurring in Lower New York Harbor exceeding the FEMA 100 year base flood elevations. Peak storm tides surpassed all previously documented high water marks, including the October 31, 1991 and December 11, 1992 nor'easters and the recorded peaks from Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Donna in 1960.||Up to 2 to 5 feet of inundation occurred in low lying areas along the Hudson River causing moderate to major damage. The towns of Stony Point and Piermont sustained the most widespread major damage. Due to the inundation, mandatory evacuations were ordered in the Grassy Point section of the Town of Stony Point along the Hudson River.  Approximately 400 people were evacuated from their homes.  Over 100 of these individuals were still not able to return to their homes 3 weeks later.  In the Village of Piermont, approximately 300 individuals were directed to evacuate their homes and businesses. Up and down the Hudson, boats pushed ashore and all manner of debris could be seen.

The National Weather Service in New York, NY confirmed an EF0 tornado with maximum winds of 80 mph in the towns of Greenwich and Stamford in Fairfield County Connecticut. The tornado touched down in the town of Greenwich on North Street just north of the Merritt Parkway. It continued east-northeast into the town of Stamford and lifted on Janes Lane approximately a half mile west of Scofieldtown Road.||Extensive tree damage was observed along the tornado path starting on Taconic Road and continuing onto Skyridge Road. The most significant tree damage was observed just south of the intersection of Stag Lane and Stanwich Road, where numerous large trees and power lines were downed. Tree damage continued on Carrington Drive and at the Mead House Farm. It reached its maximum width of 150 yards along River Bank Rd. immediately east of Newman Mills Park. The only structural damage was also reported at this point with the door to a barn being blown off.  |The tornado started to weaken as it moved into the town of Stamford just south of Web Hills Road and Lynam Road. Trees were last noted down at the far western end of Janes Lane.|||No fatalities or injuries were reported.

The National Weather Service in New York NY has confirmed a tornado from Berkeley Heights to Summit in Union County New Jersey. The tornado touched down in Berkeley Heights near the Passaic River just west of Garfield Street. It passed northeast through New Providence and lifted in Summit New Jersey near Evergreen Road.||Extensive tree damage was observed along the tornado path with the greatest damage occurring at the sewage treatment plant near Snyder Avenue in Berkeley Heights. Some of the downed trees were upon cars and houses. The National Weather Service also interviewed eyewitnesses of the tornado for additional confirmation.

A microburst occurred along a line approximately 1/4 to 1/2 mile to the right of, and approximately one minute before, the tornado which tracked from near Garfield Road in Berkley Heights to near Evergreen Road in Summit New Jersey. Based on Doppler Weather Radar data, a storm survey and information from the local media, the National Weather Service has confirmed an EF1 tornado impacted central Bergen County.||As a line of severe thunderstorms moved northeast, a portion of the line accelerated and produced a weak tornado as it moved northeast across Bergen County.||Both radar and observed damage patterns showed rotation near and at ground levels. This coupled with eyewitness reports of a tornado was the basis for confirming the tornado.||The most significant damage occurred in the George Washington Memorial Park Cemetery near the intersection of Paramus and Century Roads and in the Paramus Golf and Ridgewood Country Clubs, where dozens of trees were snapped and/or uprooted.

On Saturday, August 1, a 23-year-old Brooklyn man drowned off the waters of Westhampton Beach.  Westhampton Beach Village Police received a call about 1:40 p.m. reporting a man who was struggling to leave the waters off Rogers Beach.||Four village lifeguards pulled the man from the water onto shore, where he went into cardiac arrest. The lifeguards performed CPR on the man, and police later arrived and used an automatic external defibrillator. The man was taken by Westhampton Beach Ambulance to Peconic Bay Medical Center in Riverhead, where he was pronounced dead. Officials withheld the man's identity pending notification of relatives.

On Saturday, August 1, a young man from Brooklyn drowned when he was caught in a riptide in Long Beach.  Two swimmers were spotted having a tough time in the water amid strong rip currents at around 6:30 p.m. near the Allegria Hotel.||One of the swimmers was rescued, but the other, 23-year-old Kashawn Carlos, went under. His body was located after an extensive search-and-rescue operation in which lifeguards formed a human chain in the water.  Police say he had been submerged in the water for an hour.||Carlos was taken to South Nassau Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.||Officials say beachgoers had been warned of the rip currents as lifeguards went off-duty Saturday evening.

Tom Surdyke, 18, from Missouri died on Tuesday night June 28, after fighting for his life at Stony Brook Hospital. The West Point cadet was pulled, unresponsive, from the ocean at Coopers Beach in Southampton Village on Friday afternoon June 24th.  Mr. Surdyke was a cadet at West Point military academy.||According to a female eyewitness, Mr. Surdyke and another individual got caught in a rip current.  She said the two men were on a sandbar when one screamed for help, as he held Mr. Surdyke up out of the water. The eyewitness said no lifeguards were on duty. Someone finally ran up the beach to a man with a paddle board, she said, who went out to the two men. Both were pulled out of the water, although Mr. Surdyke was unresponsive. When they finally got Mr. Surdyke to shore, about five people began administering CPR.||Southampton Ambulance Chief Rick Fowler said a call came in at 3:58 p.m. for a swimmer in distress.  Twenty seven seconds later, a paramedic was in route to the scene, and arrived by 4:02 p.m.  The paramedic who arrived first, began using a defibrillator on the patient within 6 minutes of the call.  Twenty three minutes after taking over CPR, the patient was on his way to the Southampton Hospital.

Robert Moses State Park sustained substantial erosion mostly beginning September 3rd Saturday night and continuing until Monday night.  The worst erosion came Sunday night into Monday on the fifth of September.  During that time, beach flooding, in some cases up to the dune lines, was experienced throughout the length of the ocean front.  Specifically, significant beach erosion occurred at Robert Moses State Park on the west side from the Water Tower towards Field 2.  An initial rough estimate of 60-90 feet of shoreline was lost.   ||Additionally, Gilgo Beach within the Town of Babylon jurisdiction, suffered substantial beach erosion. There was a moderate loss of sand along Gilgo Beach with one area west of the Gilgo underpass experiencing a 6 foot scarp along 200 feet of beach, leaving little beach.
Hither Hills State Park had a significant amount of erosion, with an initial estimate of 30 feet of shoreline lost.

At Orient Point State Park, moderate erosion was experienced along the Gardiners Bay Shoreline, with some loss of boulders. Otherwise only minor flooding occurred at the park. ||Moderate beach erosion was also reported at Wildwood State Park on the north shore of the Town of Riverhead.

Based on a National Weather Service damage survey done in|conjunction with the Newburgh Fire Department, it has been |determined that an EF0 tornado went through the Balmville |neighborhood of Newburgh. The tornado originated near Albany Post |Road, to the south of the intersection with Bennet Road. A tree fell on a moving car on Albany Post Rd, killing the woman inside. The |tornado lifted near the Hudson River behind the house at 56 Susan |Drive. The tornado sheared off trees around half way to the |ground, peeled the bark off of one tree, and caused localized |convergence of uprooted trees. It also caused leaves to be |plastered on three sides of houses in the Susan Drive area. Based |on this, the tornado was classified as an EF0 tornado with an |estimated maximum wind speed of around 75 mph.

Based on a National Weather Service storm survey, done in|conjunction with the Putnam County Bureau of Emergency |Services, is been determined that an EF2 tornado with estimated |peak winds of 115 mph moved through Kent, New York. The tornado|originated near apartments at 1213 New York Route 52. It continued|down NY State Route 52, damaging some roofs in the strip mall at |the intersection of Route 52 and Farmers Mill Road, where it also|knocked down portions of the parapet above the Dunkin Donuts, and|snapped and uprooted some trees. The tornado lifted near 52 Bowen|Road in Kent. The most extensive damage was along Schuykill |Court, where dozens of large trees were uprooted and snapped, with|a convergent pattern to most of the fallen trees. Based on this |damage, the tornado was classified as an EF2, with estimated |maximum winds of around 115 mph.

Based on a National Weather Service storm survey, done in|conjunction with the Putnam County Bureau of Emergency Services,|is been determined that an EF1 tornado with estimated peak winds |of 100 mph moved along a discontinuous path through Patterson, New|York. The tornado originated along NY State Route 22, north of |the intersection with Haviland Hollow Road, near the Watchtower |Educational Center. The tornado then tracked along East Branch|Road, turned left toward Putnam Lake, then lifted near the |intersection of East Branch Road and Fairfield Drive. The storm |snapped multiple trees along its path, not all of it continuous. |The most extensive damage occurred in the general vicinity of 706|East Branch Road, where multiple trees were uprooted and snapped,|lying in a convergent pattern, and where leaves were splattered on|three sides of the house. Based on this information, the tornado|was classified as an EF1 with estimated maximum winds of 100 mph.

A 10-year old boy drowned after being pulled out by a rip current along one of the jetties near Ocean Beach Park off Edwards Boulevardin Long Beach around 6 p.m. Tuesday evening. The boy, Ramell McRae, and his slightly older 11-year-old brother, Jaquan McRae, were in the waters at Long Beach where swimming was off-limits Tuesday because lifeguards were not on duty, according to Long Beach Fire Commissioner Scott Kemins on scene. The 11-year-old brother was taken to a hospital in Oceanside, where he's in stable condition, officials said. The Coast Guard, NYPD Aviation, Nassau County Marine and Aviation, and Wantagh, Long Beach, North Cedarhurst, Inwood and East Rockaway fire departments all searched for the 10 year old boy. The search wrapped up for the day around 9 p.m. Tuesday and resumed early Wednesday before authorities ultimately called off the search. The boy's body was recovered Sunday June 24th.

A National Weather Service (NWS) Storm Survey Team, in conjunction with the Rockland County Office of Fire and Emergency Services, conducted a storm survey of the damage around Stony Point New York. Based on the results of this survey and NWS Doppler Radar the following has been determined. The tornado originated in Harriman State Park west of the Palisades Interstate Parkway and Gate Hill Road, and ended near Wilderness Drive in Stony Point. Numerous trees were uprooted and down.     The most severe damage is consistent with maximum wind speeds of around 100 MPH, |which indicates this was an EF-1 tornado.  The tornado had a maximum path width of around 100 yards and  was on the ground continuously for around one and one-half miles.

A National Weather Service (NWS) Storm Survey of damage in the town of New Castle New York was conducted in conjunction with the Westchester County Office of Emergency Management, and New Castle Police. Based on the results of this survey and NWS Doppler Radar the following results were determined.  The tornado began just west of the Taconic State Parkway, near the Hamlet of Millwood, and ended near Taylor Road south of the Hamlet of Mount Kisco. Many trees were uprooted or snapped along the path. There was also some roof damage to a few homes along the tornado's path.  The strongest damage occurred along route 100 in Millwood, with many large hardwood trees uprooted and snapped. This damage is consistent with maximum wind speeds of around 110 mph, making this an EF-1 tornado. The tornado had a maximum path width of around 300 yards and was on the ground continuously for around three and three-quarter miles.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey of damage in the Hamlet of Ronkonkoma New York was conducted in conjunction with the Town of Islip. Based on the results of this survey and NWS Doppler Radar data the following information has been determined. The tornado originated just north of the western end of Seneca Street and ended about one-eighth of a mile east of the intersection of Mohican Avenue and Seneca Street. The damage was confined to between Iroquois and Ontario streets along Mohican Avenue. Numerous homes sustained damage to siding and gutters and outdoor furniture. Trees have visibly sheared tops, and at least two or three trees were downed on cars. This damage is consistent with maximum wind speeds of around 85 mph, making this an EF-0 tornado. The tornado had a maximum path width of around 200 yards and was on the ground continuously for around 400 yards.

A National Weather Service (NWS) Storm Survey of damage was conducted with|Connecticut Emergency Management and Homeland Security and the New Canaan|and Norwalk Offices of Emergency Management in the area from New Canaan to Norwalk. Based on the results of this survey and NWS Doppler Radar data the following information has been determined. The tornado began near the intersection of Weed Street and Marshall Ridge Road in New Canaan and lifted near the intersection of Scribner Avenue and Orlando Road in Norwalk. Extensive tree damage was observed, and some of the trees fell on parked cars. The most significant damage was in New Canaan, where multiple trees were both uprooted and snapped. This damage is consistent with maximum wind speeds of around 100 mph, making this an EF-1 tornado. The tornado had a maximum path width of around 100 yards and was on the ground for around three and three-quarter miles.

After a little while they couldn���t feel their feet touching the ground, they turned around, and Lamine wasn���t there, the friend told the tabloid.||Two of the boys had already made it back to shore by the time first responders arrived on the scene at 5 p.m. on Saturday. The tornado began around one quarter of a mile east of |Wilderness Point on Wilderness Road. A circular house sustained minor |damage with glass shattered and blown nearby. A beam of the house was |lifted up a hill and dropped near another home. Several trees were |uprooted and snapped, and a shed was toppled over. A few trees were |downed at another home across the street in a convergent pattern, with |a small fence toppled over. This damage was consistent with an EF0 |tornado. The tornado continued moving to the northeast with EF0 damage |near a home on Isabella Beach Road. Many trees were uprooted and |snapped. One tree fell over and a piece of its trunk was forced several |feet into the ground. The EF0 tornado continued northeast along |Isabella Beach Road with a few trees and branches downed by the |intersection of Old Mallory Road. More significant damage occurred |about a tenth of a mile from the intersection of Old Mallory Road and |East End Road. Large hardwood trees were snapped, twisted, and sheared |off. Several trees were downed and uprooted. A large branch fell |through the roof of the garage on the property and another branch |caused minor damage to the back of the roof of the home. The damage at |this location was consistent with an EF1 tornado with estimated max |wind speeds of 90 mph. The tornado weakened to an EF0 as it continued |moving northeast. Several trees were snapped and uprooted near the |intersection of East End Road and Cedar Ridge. A small shed was also |toppled over. A few trees were downed about a tenth of a mile north of |the intersection of East End Road and Clay Point Road. This is where |the tornado moved off of Fishers island.
